title: From Protein Chips to EdTech
author: BG Eoghegan
summary: BG Eoghegan draws a precise and provocative analogy between the diet and weight-loss industry and K-12 education, arguing that both share a fatal tendency: mistaking novelty for progress, chasing the latest trend rather than adhering to foundational practices supported by decades of evidence. The trigger is a teacher friend's photo of protein-infused chips — a product that rides a trend label while delivering little real benefit — and Eoghegan uses it to trace the parallel in education: a genuine insight about technology's potential has been extrapolated into near-total classroom integration, producing passive students who disengage from anything they consider boring. The spending-outcomes parallel is damning: $135 billion on diets in 2025 with 70%+ adult obesity; $1 trillion on K-12 education with only a third of students reaching proficiency in reading or math. Eoghegan argues that the backlash against excessive screen use in schools creates an opportunity to reconsider the technology-as-progress assumption, and that the standard for adoption should be independent evidence of learning gains over non-digital alternatives — a bar most current classroom technology does not meet.
points: The diet-EdTech analogy is structural: both industries operate by extrapolating a legitimate narrow finding into a universal solution, then marketing that solution with such intensity that adoption becomes a sign of seriousness rather than a conclusion of evidence.

The spending-outcomes gap exposes the failure: $1 trillion in K-12 education spending with a third of students reaching proficiency suggests inputs are systematically misdirected toward fashionable approaches rather than effective ones.

The EdTech trend failure mirrors the low-fat era in dieting: a genuinely useful insight (reducing certain inputs has some value) was treated as a magic ingredient, ignoring that the mechanism driving benefit was absent at scale.

The backlash against screen use in schools is creating an opportunity for evidence-based reconsideration — schools willing to deploy technology only where it demonstrably outperforms non-digital alternatives could recover significant instructional time and student attention capacity.

Eoghegan's prescriptive standard — adopt EdTech only where independent research shows genuine learning gains over non-digital alternatives — is simple but would eliminate a large fraction of current classroom technology use, making it a genuinely radical rather than merely rhetorical criterion.
quotes: There are two multi-billion-dollar industries in America, and they share a lot in common. Both are quick to jump on the latest trends, both easily convince their “customers” that the evidence is undeniable, and both insist that those trends saturate every aspect of the industry. The two entities I’m referring to are the diet and weight-loss industry and the K-12 education industry.

Much like the cyclical nature of weight-loss fads, both entities have become fixated on peddling the latest breakthrough rather than adhering to foundational practices supported by decades of clear evidence. They frequently mistake novelty for genuine progress, leaving both “customers” and students to bear the ultimate cost.

It wasn’t the exorbitant amount of money spent or the lack of significant improvement that alerted me to the similarities between the diet-and-weight-loss industry and the education industry. It was actually a teacher friend who posted a picture of a protein-infused bag of chips. A high-protein diet is the latest weight-loss trend, so, naturally, everything from chips to water now contains excessive amounts of this magic ingredient that promises to satisfy hunger and build muscle.

Education has experienced a similar impulse: the belief that technology should be woven into nearly every aspect of teaching and learning. Initially, the education community celebrated computers and other technologies for the way they promised to simplify and streamline teachers’ tasks. The same community embraced educational technology for the way it got students excited about learning.

Unfortunately, in recent years, this has morphed into some teachers being unable to do their jobs effectively without the assistance of technology, and many students refusing to engage when they consider the task or assignment “boring”. It has also led to reduced learning due to the passive nature of most educational technology.

In other words, just as the fad diets weren’t inherently bad in themselves, technology in schools is not necessarily bad. How it’s used, how much schools rely on it to solve all their problems, and whether or not the technology is moving the needle on student learning are the real issues. After investing roughly $30 billion in educational technology in 2024, schools have little evidence that those expenditures produced meaningful gains in student achievement.
